stories.title: From reactive to proactive: How endpoint monitoring is fixing broken meeting rooms
stories.headline: From reactive to proactive: How endpoint monitoring is fixing broken meeting rooms
stories.summary: The role of meeting rooms is changing. Traditionally, they were formal spaces built around a large central table and inflexible physical setup, reserved primarily for board meetings, client presentations, or official status updates. The rise of hybrid work and advances in collaboration technology have made that approach increasingly obsolete.
stories.expanded:
The role of meeting rooms is changing. Traditionally, they were formal spaces built around a large central table and inflexible physical setup, reserved primarily for board meetings, client presentations, or official status updates. The rise of hybrid work and advances in collaboration technology have made that approach increasingly obsolete.

Employees now come into the office to connect, collaborate, and brainstorm with colleagues rather than to undertake the solo, focused work they can do better at home. The upshot is that many meeting rooms have transformed into fluid, digitized, data-enabled hubs. With modular partitions, movable furniture, and casual seating, they are designed to adapt to whatever task is at hand.

As digital nodes, they also bridge the gap between remote and office workers, so remote and in-person participants get a consistent experience regardless of location. That shift is only possible because of the convergence between IT and audio-visual (AV) equipment, explains Yannic Laleeuwe, marketing director for Barco's ClickShare visualization, collaboration, and networking platform. Cameras, microphones, and wireless conferencing, collaboration and presentation tools, such as ClickShare can now connect to enterprise networks.

stories.title: Rails originator roasted over Rust boosterism
stories.headline: Rails originator roasted over Rust boosterism
stories.summary: Last month at Rails World 2026, Ruby on Rails creator David Heinemeier Hansson gave a relentlessly optimistic keynote in which he suggested AI has all but eliminated the need for developers to manually write code. But perhaps DHH, as he is known online, shouldn’t delete his code editor quite yet. On Sunday, DHH posted about a test in which he had frontier agents implement and optimize his company’s Campfire group chat app in three languages: Elixir, Go, and Rust.
stories.expanded:
Last month at Rails World 2026, Ruby on Rails creator David Heinemeier Hansson gave a relentlessly optimistic keynote in which he suggested AI has all but eliminated the need for developers to manually write code. But perhaps DHH, as he is known online, shouldn’t delete his code editor quite yet. On Sunday, DHH posted about a test in which he had frontier agents implement and optimize his company’s Campfire group chat app in three languages: Elixir, Go, and Rust.

He then compared the runtime performance of those versions with the original Ruby on Rails implementation. DHH’s post includes data that seemingly demonstrates the efficiency of the Rust programming language, and AI agent coding itself. But many observers came to another conclusion: Don't trust DHH’s benchmarks.

As of press time, the post and accompanying chart garnered over 900,000 views. It showed the Rust rewrite of the chat app outperformed others by a wide margin on five tasks, including searching or posting a message. DHH did not say which AI services he used for these rewrites, but noted that each rewrite took only a few hours, as the original code itself, largely written in Ruby, is relatively compact.

stories.title: COSMIC shuts the door on AI code as GNOME debates letting bug reports in
stories.headline: COSMIC shuts the door on AI code as GNOME debates letting bug reports in
stories.summary: System76 is banning AI-generated content from contributions to the COSMIC desktop. Some GNOME sub-projects also restrict AI-generated contributions, but one developer is urging them to make an exception for vulnerability reports. The COSMIC desktop project has changed its contributors' guidelines.
stories.expanded:
System76 is banning AI-generated content from contributions to the COSMIC desktop. Some GNOME sub-projects also restrict AI-generated contributions, but one developer is urging them to make an exception for vulnerability reports. The COSMIC desktop project has changed its contributors' guidelines.

The latest version now has a clear no-AI rule, insisting that contributors declare: "I have not included any LLM (also known as AI) generated content in this PR, including code, comments, and descriptions. " In other words, you can teach yourself using AI, you can find bugs with AI, but if you want to submit your code for inclusion in COSMIC, you can't use AI to write the code, its docs or notes, or even the submission requests. This position is in keeping with some other desktop projects.

For instance, the GNOME Calendar guide to contributing says: "This project does not allow contributions generated by large languages [sic] models (LLMs) and chatbots. " GNOME Extensions also restricts AI-generated submissions, although it permits AI learning aids and code completion. Its review guidelines spell it out: "Extensions must not be AI-generated.

stories.title: Europe's mobile operators sell fewer phones but gain share as budget market shrivels
stories.headline: Europe's mobile operators sell fewer phones but gain share as budget market shrivels
stories.summary: European mobile operators are gaining a slightly larger share of smartphone sales, not because they are selling more devices, but because other sales channels are shrinking faster. This is according to market watcher Counterpoint Research, which says that sales of new smartphones through European operators were down by 4 percent during the second quarter of this year, compared with the same period a year ago. But device sales through the open market fared much worse, declining by 11 percent.
stories.expanded:
European mobile operators are gaining a slightly larger share of smartphone sales, not because they are selling more devices, but because other sales channels are shrinking faster. This is according to market watcher Counterpoint Research, which says that sales of new smartphones through European operators were down by 4 percent during the second quarter of this year, compared with the same period a year ago. But device sales through the open market fared much worse, declining by 11 percent.

This refers to phones that are bought outright from independent retailers or directly from manufacturers, which are typically SIM-free and unlocked so the customer can choose which network they hook up to. Operators accounted for 36 percent of European smartphone sales in the second quarter, up from 35 percent a year earlier. The open market still represented the majority.

As The Register has covered numerous times this year, mobile phones have been hit by the AI-driven memory crisis, which has led to a shortage of the DRAM and NAND flash components needed for consumer kit like smartphones and PCs. The resulting rise in prices has been felt most keenly at the lower end of the market, effectively making it commercially unviable to produce budget devices, according to some reports. Phones sold through operators tend to be higher-end models than those bought on the open market.

stories.title: When one datacenter is no longer enough
stories.headline: When one datacenter is no longer enough
stories.summary: Training the largest AI models is no longer simply a question of adding more GPUs. As clusters grow, power availability is becoming a hard physical constraint, forcing infrastructure teams to consider how a single training workload can operate across multiple data centres. That creates a very different networking problem.
stories.expanded:
Training the largest AI models is no longer simply a question of adding more GPUs. As clusters grow, power availability is becoming a hard physical constraint, forcing infrastructure teams to consider how a single training workload can operate across multiple data centres. That creates a very different networking problem.

Traditional datacenter interconnect was designed to move traffic between sites. AI training demands something more exacting: huge, synchronous flows, minimal packet loss and tightly coordinated communication between GPUs. If one part of the cluster stalls, the impact can ripple across the entire job.

In this interview, The Register’s Tim Phillips speaks with Rakesh Chopra, SVP, Silicon and Systems Architecture, Cisco Fellow, about what Cisco calls the “Scale-Across” imperative and why it believes distributed AI infrastructure requires a new approach to routing. Rakesh explains how the demands of AI are changing the role of the network, from simple transport to an integral part of the compute system. He discusses the challenge of making geographically separate facilities behave more like a single deterministic machine, and why buffering, high-speed coherent optics and tightly integrated silicon matter when workloads span long-distance fiber links.

stories.title: Google rolls out improved SynthID AI content detector, now available globally
stories.headline: Google rolls out improved SynthID AI content detector, now available globally
stories.summary: Every piece of AI content from Google's Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic . SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process. It's going to be a little easier going forward, though.
stories.expanded:
Every piece of AI content from Google's Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic . SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process. It's going to be a little easier going forward, though.

Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it's available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website. SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio. Google says Gemini alone has integrated SynthID with over 180 billion images and videos, plus 240,000 years of audio.

Until now, the only way for those outside of Google's trusted tester program to check for SynthID was to ask Gemini. This is rather clunky, and the model's output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple "yes" or "no. " Now you can cut Gemini out of the loop.

stories.title: Trade group crunches numbers on Trump’s impossible push for 100% US-made tech
stories.headline: Trade group crunches numbers on Trump’s impossible push for 100% US-made tech
stories.summary: One of Donald Trump’s biggest goals as president is to increase domestic manufacturing and reshore supply chains so that the most in-demand technologies in the world can be 100 percent made in the United States. By executive order last December, he launched his “Genesis Mission,” an ambitious plan seeking to leverage US dominance in AI to maintain or seize an edge in advanced robotics, biotechnology, semiconductors, and nuclear technologies. According to Trump, that plan works best with self-sustaining supply chains.
stories.expanded:
One of Donald Trump’s biggest goals as president is to increase domestic manufacturing and reshore supply chains so that the most in-demand technologies in the world can be 100 percent made in the United States. By executive order last December, he launched his “Genesis Mission,” an ambitious plan seeking to leverage US dominance in AI to maintain or seize an edge in advanced robotics, biotechnology, semiconductors, and nuclear technologies. According to Trump, that plan works best with self-sustaining supply chains.

Not even neighboring countries or longtime allies should be relied upon to manufacture a single component of any US product in his ideal world. The Consumer Technology Association (CTA) has long warned that Trump’s reshoring goals are not grounded in reality, but only recently has America’s largest technology trade association attempted to estimate what it would cost businesses and consumers to follow through on Trump’s plan. stories.title: AI/ML is becoming a performance factor in motorsport
stories.headline: AI/ML is becoming a performance factor in motorsport
stories.summary: There’s been something of a change in the world of motorsport over the past few years. It has to do with where the money comes from. In the old days, it was tobacco and, to a lesser extent, booze.
stories.expanded:
There’s been something of a change in the world of motorsport over the past few years. It has to do with where the money comes from. In the old days, it was tobacco and, to a lesser extent, booze.

Today such things are mostly banned, and when you look at a racecar covered in sponsor logos, you’re likely to see something crypto-, cyber-, or AI-related. This makes sense—an ever-larger share of our GDP is wrapped up in those segments. They’re the ones with all the money, and it takes money to go racing.

So at the amateur level, we’ve seen tech CEOs replace dentists as the privateer of choice: This past weekend’s Petit Le Mans included co-founders of GitHub, CrowdStrike, Shopify, and the creator of Ruby on Rails, to name a few. But this is an instance where a sponsor can provide tangible benefits to their motorsports partner beyond a bank transfer, as Chip Ganassi Racing (CGR) and OpenAI have been showing in IndyCar this year. stories.title: Mistral says "Le Chonk" can challenge the best AI models
stories.headline: Mistral says "Le Chonk" can challenge the best AI models
stories.summary: As tensions mount over who gets access to top-end artificial intelligence , French company Mistral has released a new freely available model that it claims can compete with the very best from the US and China. The new 1 trillion-parameter model, Mistral Large 4—nicknamed Le Chonk—can be used and customized by anyone. It’s currently available in preview, with a final version to follow by the end of the month.
stories.expanded:
As tensions mount over who gets access to top-end artificial intelligence , French company Mistral has released a new freely available model that it claims can compete with the very best from the US and China. The new 1 trillion-parameter model, Mistral Large 4—nicknamed Le Chonk—can be used and customized by anyone. It’s currently available in preview, with a final version to follow by the end of the month.

Though Le Chonk is built to compete with leading general-purpose models, it’s optimized specifically for coding and cyberdefense, as well as tasks particular to manufacturing, finance, electrical engineering, and other niches. “There are a lot of areas where the other labs will not focus that much,” Guillaume Lample, cofounder and chief scientist at Mistral, tells WIRED. “There are so many domains in which you can improve models.

AI subscriptions are heavily subsidized – customers get far more tokens for their money than they would paying metered API rates.

stories.title: South Korean president calls for creation of tools that stop all cyber-attacks
stories.headline: South Korean president calls for creation of tools that stop all cyber-attacks
stories.summary: South Korean president Lee Jae Myung has told the nation’s cabinet that it’s time to develop AI-powered defensive tools to combat AI-wielding attackers. “Recently, a series of personal information leak incidents have been occurring at financial and public institutions,” he said yesterday – likely referring to incidents like the breach at e-tailer Coupang and last week’s raid on local banks that exposed customer data. “Circumstances indicate that artificial intelligence was utilized, causing great concern and anxiety among the public,” he claimed.
stories.expanded:
South Korean president Lee Jae Myung has told the nation’s cabinet that it’s time to develop AI-powered defensive tools to combat AI-wielding attackers. “Recently, a series of personal information leak incidents have been occurring at financial and public institutions,” he said yesterday – likely referring to incidents like the breach at e-tailer Coupang and last week’s raid on local banks that exposed customer data. “Circumstances indicate that artificial intelligence was utilized, causing great concern and anxiety among the public,” he claimed.

“I request that the relevant authorities swiftly and clearly identify the circumstances of these incidents, and rapidly deploy and concentrate the necessary personnel and resources to minimize damage,” he added, before calling for South Korea’s government to “build security capabilities that can detect attacks in advance and preemptively block them. ” “I urge the relevant ministries to quickly inspect the security systems across the entire national core infrastructure, as well as the private sector, and immediately implement any necessary security measures,” he continued. “I hope we can accelerate the development and distribution of AI technologies specifically tailored for cybersecurity.

” President Lee thinks South Korea needs to “completely innovate our society's security paradigm to fit the AI era. ” That work will involve public and private sector players collaborating “to transform our technology, systems, and awareness. ” The remarks amount to a major policy statement, and a very public one at that.
